analysis.one_liner: Requires drug companies to pay Medicaid-style rebates on prescriptions filled for low-income seniors and disabled people in Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, vote, or any committee action after its April 2013 referral, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare drug plans currently pay drug makers close to full price for prescriptions filled by about nine million low-income seniors and disabled people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid — a group Medicaid itself would charge much less. This bill would have required manufacturers to pay the government a rebate on those prescriptions, calculated the same way Medicaid rebates are, with the savings returned to Medicare. Any drug company that refused to sign a rebate agreement would have its drugs excluded from Medicare's drug benefit. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2013 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income seniors and disabled people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid — the group the bill defines as 'rebate eligible individuals' — would benefit because the government would claw back rebates on their prescriptions at Medicaid-level discounts, reducing the federal cost of their drug coverage. Medicare as a whole would gain: rebates would be deposited into the Medicare prescription drug account, slowing the drain on the program's finances and, indirectly, the premiums all beneficiaries pay. Taxpayers benefit from the reduced federal spending.

how_it_helps.text: It would require drug manufacturers to pay the government a rebate, calculated using the same formula as Medicaid rebates, for every prescription dispensed to low-income people enrolled in Medicare drug plans — the roughly 9 million 'dual eligibles' who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid.
The rebates would be deposited into the Medicare prescription drug account, reducing the federal cost of the Part D program and the low-income subsidies the government pays to drug plans.

To enforce compliance, the bill excludes from Part D coverage any drug made by a company that refuses to sign a rebate agreement, and it imposes civil money penalties on insurance plans that fail to report the data needed to calculate the rebates.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers would pay the cost: they would owe the government a rebate for every covered prescription dispensed to a low-income enrollee, calculated so that they pay the gap between Medicaid's rebate formula and whatever discounts they already negotiate in Medicare. A manufacturer refusing to pay would have its drugs excluded from the Medicare drug benefit, effectively forcing participation. Drug plans and insurers would bear new reporting and audit paperwork.

drawbacks.text: The bill is coercive by design: a manufacturer that refuses to sign the rebate agreement would have its drugs excluded from Medicare Part D coverage entirely, meaning patients taking those drugs could lose access to them through their plan. Supporters accepted this tradeoff as the enforcement mechanism; opponents called it government price-setting through the back door.

The rebate amount is calculated as the difference between the Medicaid rebate and the average rebate plans already negotiate, so drug companies would pay up only when their negotiated discounts fall short of Medicaid levels — a formula that requires detailed per-drug, per-plan reporting by insurers and a new estimation and reconciliation process by HHS, adding administrative complexity for drug plans and manufacturers alike.

Savings flow to the government and lower-income enrollees' program costs rather than directly to most Part D beneficiaries' out-of-pocket costs, so the benefit to the typical senior is indirect — through the program's finances and the low-income subsidy — rather than a visible price cut at the pharmacy counter.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and large: low-income seniors and disabled Medicare enrollees would get the same discounted drug prices that Medicaid patients already get, and the Medicare program itself would save money. The main cost is borne by pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would give up revenue they currently earn on this population, and supporters of the industry's position argue that mandated rebates of this kind could lead manufacturers to raise list prices elsewhere or reduce investment in new drugs. The bill also adds reporting work for drug plans and relies on HHS to build the machinery for calculating rebates. On balance, the bill transfers money from a highly profitable industry to taxpayers and low-income beneficiaries, and its main design protection — manufacturers could keep their drugs off Part D rather than pay — is weak because leaving Part D would mean losing most of the Medicare market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2013, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote, so it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: S. 740 was introduced on April 16, 2013 by Senator John D. Rockefeller IV with 19 cosponsors and read twice before being referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

The committee referral was the last action of any kind on the bill; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

The bill would have required manufacturers to pay rebates for drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees starting in 2014-2015, with the money deposited into the Medicare prescription drug account.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: they kept charging full prices, backed by government subsidies, on drugs used by low-income Medicare beneficiaries, with no new rebate obligation. The bill's death also meant Medicare spending on this population stayed higher than it would have been.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill's last recorded action was the referral itself.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending Medicaid-style rebates to Medicare's low-income enrollees, arguing it amounted to government-mandated price controls; the industry successfully defended the Part D structure after the 2003 Medicare law barred exactly this kind of government rebate authority.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors were Democrats or Independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced beyond the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee.

industries.industry: Brand-name and other prescription drug manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would require manufacturers to pay Medicaid-style rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees — roughly the same discounts they already give Medicaid, but extended to a population where they currently collect full price backed by government payments. Refusing means having their drugs shut out of Part D, so the industry's revenue on this population would fall materially. This is the interest the bill was written against, and the bill died without a vote.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D drug plans and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Plans would take on new reporting duties with civil penalties of up to $10,000 a day for late or false data, and the government subsidies paid to plans for low-income enrollees would shrink as rebates reduced costs. Their role as the channel through which all Part D drug money flows is untouched — the bill works through them rather than around them.

industries.industry: Pharmacies and the drug supply chain
industries.note: The bill adjusts how Medicaid 'best price' and 'average manufacturer price' are calculated to avoid cascading rebate effects into Medicaid drug pricing. Retail pharmacies' reimbursement formulas are tied to these benchmarks, so the exclusion shields them from knock-on price changes but preserves a pricing system built around opaque manufacturer discounts.
